A chest X-ray is one of the most common medical imaging examinations, used to evaluate the lungs, heart, and chest wall. The heart size is within normal limits; specifically, the transverse diameter of the heart is less than half the internal diameter of the rib cage, which is the standard measure for evaluating cardiomegaly. The pleural spaces are clear, as evidenced by the sharp, well-defined costophrenic angles where the diaphragm meets the chest wall. Any fluid accumulation, known as a pleural effusion, would typically cause blunting of these angles. Additionally, there are no visible lung masses or nodules, which would be categorized as lung lesions. The bony structures, including the ribs and clavicles, appear intact without evidence of acute fractures. Several external EKG leads are visible on the patient's skin in the first image, which are standard for monitoring a patient's heart rate and rhythm during an examination but do not interfere with the interpretation of the internal structures.
